newsitem.title: USA: Grains fall on better weather, oil on Saudi rumor.
newsitem.headline: Grains fall on better weather, oil on Saudi rumor.

text.p: Grain prices fell sharply on Monday as weather forecasts pointed to better conditions for maturing corn and soybeans in the Midwest and oil prices dropped on a rumour that Saudi Arabia would increase oil sales.
In other markets, gold prices were mixed and lumber prices fell as the Commodity Research Bureau Index of 17 futures ended 1.67 points lower at 244.18.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, grain traders shrugged off news about scattered frost in northern Iowa on Saturday and sold futures contracts on speculation that forecasts for warmer temperatures later this week would help crops fill out.
December corn closed 7 cents a bushel lower at $3.14-1/2, and November soybeans closed 9 cents a bushel lower at $7.93.
"It's follow-through technical selling from the breakdown late last week and the lack of any significant cold air for the next 10 days," said Mark Cermak of O'Connor & Co.

The National Weather Service on Friday issued an outlook for above normal temperatures and below normal rainfall in the Midwest Sept. 19 through Sept. 23, growing conditions that would aid late growth in both crops.
Agronomists said frost on Saturday damaged corn and beans in low-lying fields in northern Iowa and southern Minnesota.
"The market is saying there was not a lot of damage," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.
December wheat futures closed at $4.17 a bushel, down 7 cents, after weekend news that Egypt, one of the biggest customers for U.S. wheat, bought 450,000 metric tons of wheat from France.
"Egypt buying wheat from France didn't help," Lespinasse said. "That's bearish too, the increased global competition."
At the New York Mercantile Exchange oil prices came off the boil as talk circulated that the United States had asked Saudi Arabia to increase oil output.
October crude oil closed $1.32 lower at $23.19 a barrel.
"It was definitely that Saudi story," said Tom Bentz, oil market analyst at ING Derivatives.

Oil traders said the story suggested the United States would ask Saudis to raise production to offset the postponement of the U.N.-Iraq oil-for-food deal due to the latest U.S.-Iraqi tensions. But the U.S. State Department and sources in the Mideast Gulf later denied any request had or would be made.
"We let the free market run its course in terms of supply and demand," said a U.S. State Department official.
October heating oil fell a sharp 2.65 cents a gallon to 65.29 cents and October unleaded gasoline closed 1.73 cents a gallon lower at 62.87 cents.

At the Commodity Exchange in New York, gold traders kept a wary eye on International Monetary Fund talks in Washington, which are weighing a proposal to allow sales of some 5 million ounces of the IMF's gold, when needed, to help finance aid to poor countries.
December gold closed 70 cents an ounce higher at $386.30 an ounce, but traders were downplaying the IMF's role.
"The IMF issue is already built into the price," said Ian McDonald, vice presdient at Credit Suisse. "In reality, 5 million ounces is nothing."
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange November lumber futures ended locked down the $10 daily limit for a second consecutive trading day at $351 per thousand board feet.

The November to January period is usually slower for the lumber market as winter weather curbs construction projects in some parts of the United States. Weakness in cash markets has begun changing the long-running bullishness of traders.
"By mid- to late week you are going to see much lower lumber prices," said Neil Schmaedick, Smith Barney Forest Products analyst.
